# Tool recipe (v2)

Schema for `.tera/tools/<name>.hcl` recipes per PRD-012 §4.4.3. Mirrors `pkg/systemvault/loader.ToolSpec`. A tool is a vault-resident process (executable + supporting files) or a bundled tool — a binary installed beside `tera` and named bare, which is how the `claude-code` harness adapter ships (ADR-110 D1 Amendment 1).

| | |
|---|---|
| Registry name | `recipe/tool` |
| Regime | persisted |
| Identity regime | `recipe` — the filename stem is the identity; the file declares exactly one resource, and a block label — where the grammar admits one — must equal the stem (ADR-087 D3) |
| Current version | `v2` |
| Supported versions | `v1`, `v2` |
| Schema `$id` | `https://kottera.dev/schemas/recipe/tool/v2` |
| Go source | `github.com/kottera/kottera/pkg/systemvault/schemas.toolRecipe` |
| Served at | `GET /api/v1/schemas/recipe/tool/{version}` |
| JSON Schema | `GET /api/v1/schemas/recipe/tool/v2` |

## Example

A minimal `tool`: every required attribute, exactly one member of each closed union, and nothing optional beyond what the kind would otherwise render empty. It is generated from the same source these tables are, and the same bytes are run through `tera validate` by the ADR-087 D9 pattern-transfer test — so it cannot describe a shape the loader does not accept.

Cross-references name the other kinds' examples (`example-worker`, `example-tool`, …) because every kind's example is validated together with the rest, as one vault.

`.tera/tools/example-tool.hcl`:

```hcl
version = "v2"

tool "example-tool" {
  description = "What this is for, in one line."
  runtime     = "exec"
  entry       = "run.sh"
}
```

## Attributes

| Attribute | Type | Required | Default | Since | Constraints | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `version` | string | yes | — | — | const `v2` | Per-recipe grammar version. Required. v2 is current: it replaced the mcp_servers server credential ATTRIBUTE with the credential { spec \| filer } block union (ADR-135 D19). A v1 recipe still loads with no edit — the loader migrates it on read and the attribute becomes credential { spec "<name>" {} }, which is what it always meant — so this value is what a NEW recipe declares rather than a thing an existing one has to be changed to. |
| `name` | string | yes | — | — | min length 1 | Bare tool name (the HCL block label). The loader namespaces it as <vault-id>/tools/<name>. |
| `description` | string | no | — | — | — | Human-readable description surfaced in operator UIs. |
| `runtime` | string | no | — | — | — | Dispatch runtime. Empty defaults to exec. Recognised values include exec, native, bash, sh. |
| `handler` | string | no | — | — | — | A bare filename (no separator, no colon) selects a bundled tool — a binary installed beside the tera that dispatches it, resolved at <install>/libexec/<goos>-<goarch>/<name> with a flat <install>/libexec/<name> fallback, and overridable by the packager env var TERA_LIBEXEC_DIR. Resolution happens on whichever host runs the dispatch, so a runner uses its own install rather than the daemon's. Empty/unset selects the vault-resident process at <dir>/<entry>. |
| `entry` | string | no | — | — | — | Relative path inside the per-tool directory to the executable. Defaults to run.sh. Mutually exclusive with a handler the dispatching host resolves (a bundled bare name), which has no vault-resident file for an entry to point into. |
| `source` | block | no | — | — | — | Client-side build declaration (PRD-014 C3, ADR-061 §5). Advisory only: the daemon never builds from it; the resolved executable is always the on-disk artifact. |
| `timeout` | string | no | — | — | — | Top-level shorthand for sandbox.timeout (Go duration, e.g. 45m). |
| `input_schema` | string | no | — | — | — | Raw JSON Schema for invocation arguments (heredoc body in HCL). Set "x-tera-stdin": true on one top-level string property to declare it the tool's stdin sink — the property a shell pipeline's standard input binds to when the tool is invoked as a command (ADR-073 D2). Absent that annotation nothing binds from stdin and piping into the command is an error; a sink is never inferred. |
| `output_schema` | string | no | — | — | — | Raw JSON Schema for the tool's result (heredoc body in HCL). Optional and symmetric with input_schema (ADR-074 D1). Omit it to declare nothing — absence is honest, and no placeholder schema is inferred on your behalf. |
| `config_schema` | string | no | — | — | — | Raw JSON Schema for per-binding configuration. IT MUST BE SELF-CONTAINED: an internal reference (#/$defs/...) is fine, and any $ref the compiler would have to fetch or read off the daemon's disk is refused, because the recipe is the declaration and a schema whose meaning lives in a second file is one no vault carries, no config plan diffs and no reviewer sees. |
| `config_defaults` | object | no | — | — | — | Lowest-precedence ordinary binding configuration. Fixed sites may replace complete top-level values; nested objects are never recursively merged (ADR-131 D7). |
| `credential_spec` | block (list) | no | — | — | — | Declares the credential interface this tool consumes. Workers supply concrete values via capability_credentials blocks. |
| `sandbox` | block | no | — | — | — | Sandbox execution limits and network posture. |
| `credentials` | map<string, string> | no | — | — | — | Maps credential binding names to definition-level default values. A value is dereferenced when it carries a supported reference scheme (env://VAR, keychain://service[#json.path], vault://path) and is otherwise the secret itself. A value carrying a scheme this daemon cannot act on is REFUSED at resolution rather than injected as its own text (#2897): file:// most sharply, which IS a credential reference on the client side (tera context, tera trace tail --api-key) and is not one here, because the daemon would be reading an arbitrary host path on behalf of a recipe. So is a scheme one edit from a supported one (keychan://, envv://, vualt://), which is a typo rather than a secret. Everything else is still a literal, so a postgres:// connection string needs nothing special; prefix a value with literal:// to say a scheme-carrying value is the secret itself. |
| `env` | map<string, string> | no | — | — | — | Environment variables the dispatched process needs in order to behave — the tool's own quirks, declared by the tool rather than compiled into the daemon (#1319). A value may reference ${workspace}, the absolute writable workspace root (HOME); the process cwd may be its repo child, and the runtime selects TMPDIR separately from private scratch, or ${volume.<label>}, the host path of the volume bound at one of this tool's own volumes { volume "<label>" } requirements — which is how a cache is kept out of a workspace a ttl retains (#1849). Those two are the entire substitution vocabulary, and an unknown ${...} token fails the dispatch rather than expanding to empty; a ${volume.<label>} naming a requirement this tool does not declare is one such unknown. A declared requirement no binding satisfies expands to the workspace root instead of failing — required = true is how a tool says an absent binding must refuse the dispatch, and that refusal happens before expansion — so a value spelled ${volume.scratch}/.cache/x reads as the ${workspace}/.cache/x it replaced when nothing bound it. Three names are refused rather than silently losing a precedence race: one the runtime sets (PATH, HOME, TMPDIR, TMPPREFIX, SHLVL, LANG — TMPPREFIX is where zsh stages a here-document, which it takes from that name and never from TMPDIR, and SHLVL is what stops a top-level bash from sourcing the host's bashrc), one in a reserved namespace (TERA_*, KPP_*), and one colliding case-insensitively with one of the tool's credentials — declared env can never mask an injected credential, including a credential consumed by an api_proxy and therefore never placed in the environment at all. |
| `network` | block | no | — | — | — | Egress allow-list. Active when sandbox.network is scoped. |
| `api_proxies` | block | no | — | — | — | REFUSED at load by name (ADR-152 D7): a tool no longer presents a credential through its own proxy routes. The credential is a connection, which the dispatch's proxy presents outside the sandbox; the toolchain that supplies the client carries a connection block pointing the client's variables at that proxy; and a holder (a worker's connection binding, or a pool member naming its connection) supplies it. A recipe declaring this block does not register, at load, at tera config plan and apply and by tera validate, and a tool definition carrying it by another route is refused at dispatch and at a runner's Accept; the refusal names docs/ops/upgrade-to-connections.md#take-a-derived-tool-recipe-off-api_proxies. It is refused, not lowered: no route is rewritten into a connection. The member stays in this schema only because the recipes contract's published levels carry it (ADR-143 D3). A toolchain's provision block keeps its own api_proxies, which is a different consumer. |
| `cli_shims` | block | no | — | — | — | REFUSED at load by name (ADR-148 D4): a CLI now reaches its credential through the dispatch's proxy, outside the sandbox, so the shim and the credential agent's shim role are gone. A recipe declaring this block does not register, at load, at tera config plan and by tera validate, and the refusal names docs/ops/upgrade-to-connections.md. Nothing inside the block is parsed, and it is not migrated mechanically: what replaces it is a toolchain supplying the CLI and, on each work-order type that runs it, toolchains = ["<toolchain>"] and a connection block choosing whose credential it uses. The member stays in this schema only because the recipes contract's published levels carry it (ADR-143 D3). |
| `mcp_servers` | block | no | — | — | — | MCP servers the sandboxed process may reach through a daemon-side bridge that attaches the credential outside the sandbox. Runtime-facing, like api_proxies — never a config_schema field, so the credential does not transit the handler-facing class. |
| `volumes` | block | no | — | — | — | Data-volume mount requirements for the tool. |
| `toolchains` | string[] | no | — | — | — | Provisioned toolchain stores every dispatch of this tool mounts read-only, by bare toolchain name (ADR-109 D14). A requirement has TWO HOMES and THE WORK-ORDER TYPE IS THE NORMAL ONE: it knows what the WORK needs, so frontend work declares a browser and backend work on the same daemon through the same tool does not. What belongs here is only what is true of the tool in EVERY dispatch — claude-code needs its harness, and that is not a property of any particular work. A requirement written here that is really the work's makes every dispatch mount a store most of them will not open. A dispatch acquires the UNION of the two homes, with the tool's ordered FIRST — the tool's requirements hold for every dispatch while the work's are the local addition, and that ordering is what makes the composed environment deterministic rather than a function of which declaration the daemon read first. A NAME AND NOTHING ELSE, because a consumer of a toolchain says only which: the store is deployment-wide, no invocation supplies a binding, and the definition owns the version key, the provisioning command and what the toolchain contributes to the environment. The name resolves in this tool recipe's own vault, else in the system vault (ADR-147 D6): a vault that declares the name gets its own definition for its own tools, and a system-vault tool always gets the system vault's. Another vault's toolchain is named qualified, <vault>/toolchains/<name>, and resolves only when that vault is granted share toolchains (invoke on vaults/share/toolchains). Each vault's definition has its own store and lock entry, keyed <name>@<vault> outside the system vault. The name may not contain '@'. A name no definition declares REFUSES THE DISPATCH by name rather than mounting nothing, because a silently absent store is a wrong answer at the far end of a long dispatch. Default: empty, which mounts no store and contributes nothing. |
| `host_binaries` | string[] | no | — | — | — | Commands every dispatch of this tool expects to find ALREADY INSTALLED on whichever host runs it (ADR-106 D8, kottera/kottera#3634). A host that cannot resolve one REFUSES THE DISPATCH BEFORE anything is provisioned for it — before the workspace, before a pool member is drawn, and on a fleet before the far host touches anything local — naming the host, the missing names, the search path it looked on and the repair. Without it a missing binary is discovered INSIDE the session, as a command not found partway through, with nothing to check beforehand and nothing attributing it to the machine. THE CLAIM IS PRESENCE AND ONLY PRESENCE: not a version, not a build, not a provenance. A tool that needs a PARTICULAR build declares a toolchain instead, which is provisioned per host by an operator, versioned by a deployment-wide lock and mounted read-only to the dispatch; this is the weaker claim underneath it, and keeping it weak is what stops it becoming a lockfile with none of a lockfile's guarantees. DO NOT DECLARE THE SAME PROGRAM IN BOTH: a toolchain is carried TO the host, while a name here asserts what the host already had, so a name that a declared toolchain supplies belongs only in toolchains — the refusal says so, naming the toolchains this recipe declares. A BARE COMMAND NAME AND NOTHING ELSE: an entry containing a path separator is refused at load, because it is a path rather than a PATH lookup and the two are answered by different mechanisms. Names are resolved against the same search path the dispatch is spawned with, which is PER PLATFORM — the darwin floor reaches Homebrew and the linux floor reaches Homebrew-on-Linux and the distro paths — so a name resolvable on one host in a mixed fleet is exactly what this declaration exists to stop being assumed of the other. Default: empty, which asserts nothing about any host and is what every recipe that does not shell out to an external CLI should keep. |
| `checkpoints` | block | no | — | — | — | What an invocation of this capability reports WHILE IT RUNS (ADR-095 D6): the closed set of phases it may report, and the JSON Schema for the domain payload. This is the second of the declaration's two homes and it governs an invocation that is NOT bound to a Work Order — a gateway-invoked import, a volume sync, a direct call through an exposure. A Work-Order-bound invocation takes its work-order type's declaration instead, because the type is what knows the progression of that particular kind of work; the two are selected between and never merged, so a bound invocation whose type declared nothing is refused even where this block is present. Omitting the block is the default and means no phase is legal: nothing is inferred for a capability that has not said what its work reports. Omitting it and declaring phases = [] are both refusals and are deliberately distinguishable — the second says the author considered the question. The set is CLOSED and there is no catch-all phase, which is the mechanism rather than a validation nicety: with a closed vocabulary and no free-text field to narrate into, progress chatter is unreachable rather than discouraged, and the repair for a phase the author did not foresee is to declare it. Nothing carries a checkpoint from a running capability to the emit path yet (that is a later wave); the validation is not inert and applies to any checkpoint that reaches it today. |
| `acp` | block | no | — | — | — | Everything an ACP harness adapter needs in order to drive THIS PARTICULAR HARNESS (ADR-115 D1). Declaring it is what makes a recipe an ACP binding: the daemon merges the block into the handler-facing binding config under the reserved acp key, and acp-handler refuses a dispatch that arrives without one. THE BLOCK EXISTS SO THAT A NEW ACP HARNESS IS A RECIPE RATHER THAN A RELEASE. One acp-handler binary serves every ACP harness, so everything that differs between harnesses is declared here instead of compiled into that binary, and a new binding hot-reloads per PRD-012 with no daemon change. THE PER-HARNESS METHODS ARE EXPLICITLY UNSTABLE and that is the argument FOR this form rather than against it: _goose/unstable/session/steer says so in its own name and it will move, and when it does the repair is an edit to this block that hot-reloads, not a Go change behind a release for the sake of a string. IF YOU ARE HERE BECAUSE A METHOD MOVED, this is the file to edit and nothing else needs rebuilding. NOTHING IN THIS BLOCK IS OPTIONAL-WITH-A-DEFAULT: every attribute is required, because each is a place where an absent declaration and a declared value would be indistinguishable downstream — an absent capacity and capacity = "none" say the same thing to a scheduler and different things about the author — and the whole of ADR-115 is about refusing arrangements in which a binding silently degrades to less than it said. An empty list is always spellable and always means something; silence is not offered as a synonym for it. THE VERB BLOCKS AND in_flight.accepts MAY NOT DISAGREE: in_flight.accepts is the single answer to WHETHER a verb is offered, read by the daemon, and acp.verb says only HOW to perform one, read by the handler. A recipe declaring a verb in one and not the other is refused at load, naming both sides — because a verb accepted and unmapped is a message the daemon takes and the handler cannot deliver, and a verb mapped and unaccepted is a mapping nothing will ever call. Default: absent, which is every capability that is not an ACP binding. |
| `in_flight` | block | no | — | — | — | What this capability accepts while an invocation of it is already running (ADR-095 D1). Omitting the block is the default and means it accepts nothing: guidance addressed to such a capability is refused by name, never accepted and quietly dropped, because a message the caller believes landed in a run that never saw it reads exactly like a message that worked. Omitting the block and declaring accepts = [] are both refusals and are deliberately distinguishable — the second says the author considered the question. Declaring a verb is inert as of ADR-095 WI-A in the sense that nothing delivers a message yet; the refusal is not inert and applies today. |
| `attendable` | boolean | no | — | — | — | Whether this tool's handler implements the ATTENDED contract (ADR-179 D2): it can run its dispatch as one process in a terminal a person attaches to. DECLARING IT MAKES NO DISPATCH ATTENDED — it states that one MAY be, and a work_order_type asks for it by declaring attended {} on its own capability or select site. A tool offering what no type requests is an ordinary tool. A type requesting what this tool does not offer is REFUSED AT LOAD — at tera config validate, at config apply and at the daemon's own load — naming both files. On a select site every candidate's tool must offer it. THE OFFER IS PINNED: it is frozen into the configuration pin on a fixed site and on each pinned select candidate, so withdrawing it changes what runs next and not a session already pinned (ADR-105 D1). Default: false. |
| `subject` | block (list) | no | — | — | — | Which of THIS tool's invocation arguments carry a <kind>/<id> WORLD subject (ADR-100 D6 Amendment 1). The second home of a block whose first is the work_order_type, in checkpoints' shape and under checkpoints' rule: the two are selected between and never merged, and a Work-Order-bound dispatch takes its type's declaration. It exists because the type was the only thing that could supply subjects — a dispatch with no Work Order has no declared set at all, which is exactly why the PULL verb makes such a caller name its subjects on every read. Push has no caller to name them, so without this an observations block on a tool recipe would resolve about nothing and be inert precisely where the design most needs it. It buys a second thing besides: a no-Work-Order dispatch's observe writes are today off_subject BY DEFINITION, because there is no declared set to be on-subject with respect to, and giving that dispatch a declared set makes ADR-100 D8's volume signal mean the same thing on both paths. Repeated: the block label names an input_schema property, and a recipe declares at most four — the bound is four on both sides of a conjunctive match, because work needing five simultaneous referents is work about a situation. Three states bind nothing and all three are legitimate: no block, an absent or null argument, and the empty string. A present non-string value, a value that is not <kind>/<id>, a kind the deployment has not declared as a subject_kind recipe, and a kind outside this block's own kinds list each REFUSE rather than producing a dangling binding. A label naming a property input_schema does not declare is a load error, as is a fifth block and as are two blocks naming one input. |
| `claim` | block (list) | no | — | — | — | Which subjects an invocation of this capability must HOLD before it runs (ADR-101 D2-D8) — as against the subject block beside it, which is what the invocation is ABOUT. A claim is a durable lease over a <kind>/<id> subject, held by a principal within a scope, and unlike an index binding it GATES: an invocation requiring a subject somebody else holds does not proceed. This is the second of the declaration's two homes and it is the one ADR-101 D4 says the design most needs — THE GENERAL CASE HAS NO WORK ORDER, since most work in a building-automation or field-service deployment is a capability dispatch reached over MCP or fired by a trigger predicate, and a Work-Order-only claim would be unreachable from exactly the deployments the lockout case comes from. THE TWO HOMES COMPOSE RATHER THAN BEING SELECTED BETWEEN, which is a deliberate departure from checkpoints, observations and in_dispatch: for a push policy a selection's failure mode is a run that was not told something, and for a requirement it is a capability that declared a HARD LOCKOUT being dispatched under a work-order type that declared none, and running unclaimed. So a Work-Order-bound invocation of this capability acquires the union — this recipe's requirements AND its type's — and the bound is unaffected, because four bounds the subjects of ONE requirement rather than the number of requirements. Repeated, and the block label names the requirement. THREE AXES HAVE NO DEFAULT AND MUST BE WRITTEN: hardness, scope and on_park; hardness is the one ADR-101 D5 singles out, because a maintenance lockout that fails open because nobody typed the word is a machine that energises while someone is inside it, and a default would be silently wrong in the common direction. A requirement names its subjects literally in subjects or by operand in subject_inputs, at most four across the two and at least one, because a requirement naming none acquires nothing while reading as an interlock. THIS HOME ACQUIRES AT ITS OWN MOMENT AND THAT IS WHY THE TWO COMPOSE WITHOUT A SHARED PLAN: a work-order type's requirements are acquired at the pre-dispatch gate, atomically with scheduled to active, and a capability recipe's are acquired at the DISPATCH SEAM — before credentials resolve, before a volume is provisioned, before a sandbox is spawned — and released when the invocation ends. So a Work-Order-bound invocation of a claim-declaring capability holds both, which is the union, delivered by two moments rather than by one plan. TWO RULES ARE THIS HOME'S OWN AND ARE REFUSED AT LOAD, because the moment they would be acquired at never arrives here. scope MUST BE dispatch: the wider lifetimes name a holder and a release edge that belong to the pre-dispatch gate, which resolves a work_order_type's requirements and never a capability's, and operator is held by a person no dispatch can act for. And a requirement here names ONE SUBJECT: ADR-101 D6 acquires a set all-or-nothing, which costs the gate no code because D3 puts the acquisition inside a transaction, and a capability dispatch has no transaction to roll back. Both refusals name the two repairs — narrow the declaration, or move it to the work_order_type, where the wider shapes already work. |
| `observations` | block | no | — | — | — | What an invocation of this capability is TOLD about its own subjects, unbidden (ADR-100 D6) — the mirror of checkpoints, which is what an invocation REPORTS. This is the second of the declaration's two homes and it governs an invocation that is NOT bound to a Work Order — a gateway-invoked import, a direct call through an exposure, a sandboxed tool an external harness drove. That consumer is the one the push half most exists for: push is here because a model that does not know observations exist will never call the verb, and the consumer that needs it most is the one with no prompt and no Work Order. A Work-Order-bound invocation takes its work-order type's declaration instead; the two are SELECTED BETWEEN AND NEVER MERGED, so a bound dispatch whose type declared nothing gets no push even where this block is present. Omitting the block is the default and is no push: nothing is inferred for a capability that has not asked to be told anything. The subjects it resolves about are this recipe's own subject blocks. LIVE SINCE WAVE 3 ITEM 4 of PLAN-2026-08-learned-operational-knowledge: a dispatch of a type declaring this block IS pushed what is known about its subjects, rendered per mode into whichever driver runs it — a section of the coding harness's own CLAUDE.md, or a section of the tera-native agent's system prompt. THE TWO BOUNDS ARE LIVE TOO, since Wave 3 item 6: past max_full a render stops being full and becomes summary with the reason stated, the set itself untouched at that step, and past max_summary a summary render delivers what fits — the strongest and most recently held, ordered by confidence and then recency — and REPORTS THE COUNT IT ELIDED. THE TWO COMPOSE, so a full set past both degrades AND elides and each fact is named separately. Neither trims silently, the reason rides on the payload the driver serializes rather than only reaching the operator's log, and the D7 delivery record carries the EFFECTIVE mode with degraded saying the unit had asked for more. |

## `source` block

| Attribute | Type | Required | Default | Since | Constraints | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `language` | string | no | — | — | one of `go`, `script` | Build strategy. go cross-compiles a vendored Go module hermetically; script packages an interpreter script. |
| `path` | string | no | — | — | — | Source root, relative to the tool directory. Defaults to the tool directory. |
| `package` | string | no | — | — | — | Go only: the package to build, relative to path. Defaults to the module root. |
| `interpreter` | string | no | — | — | — | Script only: the interpreter to check for availability (e.g. python3, node). Falls back to the shebang when empty. |
| `targets` | string[] | no | — | — | — | NARROWS the deployment's declared build-target set for this one recipe, as <os>/<arch> platforms. Omitting it — the normal case — means whatever the deployment declares, which is what almost every recipe wants. IT EXISTS FOR THE CROSS-LANGUAGE CEILING: Go cross-compiles trivially and a script is near platform-neutral, but a tool with CGO or a native dependency does not cross-compile from one host, and a build that silently produces three good overlays and one broken one is worse than one that refuses the fourth by name. tera tool build refuses a declared target this list excludes, naming the target and this set, instead of handing the toolchain a build it will botch. IT IS A CEILING NARROWED BY INTERSECTION AND NEVER A WIDENING: a platform named here that the deployment does not declare is not built, because which platforms a deployment has is not one recipe's to decide. |

## `credential_spec` block

Repeatable.

| Attribute | Type | Required | Default | Since | Constraints | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `name` | string | yes | — | — | min length 1 | Credential binding name workers must supply. |
| `description` | string | no | — | — | — | Human-readable description of the credential purpose. |
| `required` | boolean | no | — | — | — | Whether the tool refuses to run without this credential. |
| `sensitive` | boolean | no | — | — | — | Whether the value must be redacted in logs and telemetry. |
| `write_back` | boolean | no | — | — | — | Whether a dispatch may hand the platform a REPLACEMENT for this credential, and the platform must therefore be able to keep one (ADR-110 D5 Amendment 2). Default false, which is the behaviour every capability had before this attribute existed: nothing acquires a requirement by it being added, and a recipe that leaves it unset produces exactly the served definition it produced before. IT IS A STATEMENT ABOUT THE SUPPLY AND NOT ABOUT THE HARNESS. A rotating credential is safely usable only when the value handed to the dispatch can be written back somewhere, which is a property of where the value came from rather than of the string, so declaring it here imposes rules on how a member may supply it — all of them refused when the configuration is composed, before any dispatch, because a harness that rotated its credential and got no error is entitled to believe the platform kept it. THE ONE LEGAL SHAPE is a pool member supplying the field from a writable encrypted secret://<name> row, with resolve_on left at its server default. env://, keychain://, vault://, literal:// and a bare literal are readable references and none of them is a writable sink; resolve_on = "runner" is refused when the recipe loads, because a host-resolved value is read on the executing host from that host's own references and the daemon never learns which one won. A definition-level credentials {} default, a worker's capability_credentials binding and a tool_binding's credentials {} override are refused too — not for being unreadable but for being unattributed: none names a member, so none serialises the write or leaves anything to hold when it fails. THE MEMBER CARRIES THREE RULES OF ITS OWN: it declares seats = 1, because an unset seats is UNBOUNDED concurrency rather than one and would admit any number of dispatches racing to rotate one document (seats = 0, a ceiling of zero, is legal and admits no lease at all); it supplies at most ONE write-back credential, because one seat lease cannot order two independent rotations; and no two members may point at one secret:// row when either rotates it, because a rotating document has one owner and every other member pointing at it is handed a document invalidated without its knowledge. More capacity is more independently enrolled members with independent rows. On a toolchain provision block the attribute is spellable and never satisfiable — a provisioning step resolves from the definition's own static credentials map and holds no member — so it is refused there when the definition loads. |
| `resolve_on` | string | no | `server` | — | one of `(empty)`, `server`, `runner` | WHERE this credential's value is resolved (ADR-028 Amendment 2, ADR-106 D8 as amended 2026-08-28) — a separate axis from WHICH supplied value wins, which is the unchanged three-tier precedence of ADR-028 section 3. The two are orthogonal, and the tempting collapse is wrong: a host-resolved credential is not a fourth tier, it does not out-rank or under-rank a worker binding, it is the same tier structure resolved somewhere else. server, the default, is a DISPATCH CREDENTIAL: the daemon resolves it through the same path a local dispatch already uses and delivers it per dispatch. This is the golden path. runner is a HOST-LOCAL FACT: it is resolved on the host that executes the dispatch, from that host's own references. RUNNER MEANS THE HOST EXECUTING THIS DISPATCH, NOT A REMOTE HOST — in a deployment with no runners at all, a credential marked runner resolves on the daemon's own machine, because that is the host executing the dispatch. The classification is a property of the CREDENTIAL and not of the host: a subscription token is a workload credential on every machine and a local CA bundle path is a host fact on every machine, which is why this is declared here on the capability's own contract rather than on a per-host file where it would have to be repeated and could disagree. Empty means server, and that default is chosen rather than inherited — nothing regresses because the host-resolved path supplies nothing today, it makes the arrangement that works the one an author gets without deciding, and an unmarked credential silently resolving host-side is the multi-host credential defect wearing a default. The cost is named rather than hidden: a credential that genuinely IS a host fact must say so, or it silently centralises, and that cost is paid by the recipe author, who knows the answer. A value outside the closed set is refused when the recipe loads, naming the credential and quoting the value. |

## `sandbox` block

| Attribute | Type | Required | Default | Since | Constraints | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `mode` | string | no | — | — | — | Sandbox enforcement mode. |
| `cpu_limit` | string | no | — | — | — | CPU-time ceiling for the sandboxed process, as a WHOLE NUMBER OF CPU-SECONDS and no unit suffix: 600, or 600.0. There is no duration spelling here even though timeout one attribute away takes one, and 1m is refused rather than read as a minute; a fractional value is refused too, because the ceiling lands on RLIMIT_CPU, which counts whole seconds, and 0.5 has nothing to become but 0 — which means no ceiling at all. A value this grammar cannot read is REFUSED, at tera validate and when the recipe loads, never converted. ENFORCED ON LINUX ONLY (RLIMIT_CPU). On darwin it is accepted and bounds nothing: Seatbelt has no CPU-time primitive and the backend applies no rlimits, so the daemon reports every recipe declaring it at boot rather than leaving the declaration to read as a ceiling. Use timeout, which is enforced everywhere. |
| `mem_limit` | string | no | — | — | — | Memory ceiling for the sandboxed process, as a unit-bearing size: 512MB, 4GB, 2Gi, 900MiB, 1.5GB. SI and IEC spellings mean the same bytes — 2GB and 2Gi are both 2*1024^3 — so the spelling used by a ceiling profile's memory and a toolchain's measured_size works here too. A value this grammar cannot read is REFUSED, at tera validate and when the recipe loads, never converted: before kottera/kottera#3334 an unrecognised spelling silently kept a multiplier of 1, and 2Gi bounded the dispatch at two bytes. ENFORCED ON LINUX ONLY — cgroup-v2 memory.max where a delegated subtree is available, RLIMIT_DATA otherwise. On darwin it is accepted and bounds nothing: Seatbelt has no memory-ceiling primitive and the backend applies no rlimits, so the daemon reports every recipe declaring it at boot rather than leaving the declaration to read as a ceiling. On such a host the dispatch is bounded by timeout and nothing else. |
| `timeout` | string | no | — | — | — | Execution ceiling for the dispatch (Go duration). The one limit enforced identically on every platform, because the daemon performs the kill itself rather than asking the host for it. ITS CLOCK STARTS WHEN THE HANDLER IS CONFIRMED STARTED — the credential agent's acknowledgement that it has spawned the handler, or the sandbox leader's start on a dispatch with no agent — so none of the launch before that (sandbox spawn, credential-agent start, handler exec) is charged to it: handshake_timeout bounds the launch separately, and a slow launch fails as handshake_timeout, never as this timeout. IT IS MEASURED ON THE MONOTONIC CLOCK OF THE HOST RUNNING THE DISPATCH, NOT ON A WALL CLOCK — mach_absolute_time on darwin, CLOCK_MONOTONIC on linux, neither of which advances while the machine is suspended. So TIME THE HOST SPENDS ASLEEP DOES NOT COUNT AGAINST IT: on a fleet host that sleeps overnight a 2h ceiling can span days of calendar time, without limit, while the dispatch holds its seat and its workspace throughout. That direction is deliberate rather than incidental — a suspended dispatch makes no progress and burns no tokens, and a fleet host is a laptop — so size this against how much WORKING time the dispatch may have rather than against how long you are willing to wait, and read a run that outlived it on a wall clock as this property rather than as a broken timeout. A dispatch's own duration_ms log lines are on the same clock, so they agree with the ceiling and disagree with the watch. |
| `network` | string | no | — | — | one of `(empty)`, `false`, `true`, `scoped` | Network posture. scoped activates the network egress allow-list. |
| `handshake_timeout` | string | no | — | — | — | Ceiling on the dispatch's LAUNCH (Go duration; 10s when unset): from the start of the dispatch until its handler is confirmed started — the credential agent's acknowledgement that it has spawned the handler, or the sandbox leader's start on a dispatch with no agent. A launch that overruns it is torn down and fails as handshake_timeout, naming the phase it was stuck in. It is independent of timeout and is never clamped to it: timeout's clock starts only when this one ends, so one dispatch lives for at most the sum of the two. |
| `read` | string[] | no | — | — | — | Filesystem read request: v1 tokens (any, workspace, tool_scratch, skill_dir) or absolute paths. Omitted requests any, which is what every tool asked for before this attribute existed; an empty list requests nothing beyond the sandbox floor. The ceiling still decides (ADR-069 D5). |
| `write` | string[] | no | — | — | — | Filesystem write request, same vocabulary and same defaults as read. Narrowing it is recorded and intersected but does not confine anything yet: writes are bounded by the working directory plus declared volume mounts, and no backend consumes the write tokens. See PRD-012 section 4.4.5. |
| `platform_grants` | string[] | no | — | — | — | Platform-grant request: named, versioned bundles of platform-native sandbox clauses that are not filesystem paths. Omitted denies, and an empty list denies the same way — the opposite of read and write, which default to any, because this axis never had a synthesized value to preserve (ADR-103 D3). The ceiling still decides, and every ceiling the daemon ships grants no token. The vocabulary is closed: a token no backend registers is refused when the recipe loads, while a registered token this platform cannot honour is refused at dispatch, so a vault stays portable. The registered tokens and the exact clauses each expands to are generated into docs/reference/platform-grants.md; a set is minimal jointly and there is no way to request part of one. |

It is a wrapper holding exactly one variant block, spec or filer, and a server declaring neither or both is refused at load. AT TOOL GRAMMAR v1 THIS WAS AN ATTRIBUTE, credential = "<spec-name>", and a v1 recipe still loads unedited: the v1 to v2 migration rewrites it to credential { spec "<spec-name>" {} }, which is what it always meant. The attribute is not kept beside the block, because an attribute-or-block pair would be a new field-presence union and ADR-087 section 5 closes those at two. Whichever arm is declared, the credential's VALUE is attached outside the sandbox and the sandboxed process never holds it. |

## `mcp_servers.server.credential` block

Nested under `mcp_servers.server`.

| Attribute | Type | Required | Default | Since | Constraints | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `spec` | block | no | — | — | — | Attach a credential_spec declared on this same tool, named in the block label. The principal the far side sees follows from whatever the WORKER'S BINDING resolves that spec to, which is what lets one tool spec serve several agents with different principals. This is what every pre-v2 credential = "<name>" attribute meant. Exactly one of the spec or filer blocks must be declared (ADR-087 D4). |
| `filer` | block | no | — | — | — | Attach the DELEGATION SUBJECT'S credential: the person who filed the Work Order this dispatch belongs to (ADR-135 D4). The daemon presents a per-dispatch token minted from its own issuer and the gateway sees a caller whose principal is that person, so token selection, tool filtering and audit all key on them rather than on the worker. It is not impersonation and it grants nothing: the delegation subject decides which DELEGATED TOKENS a dispatch may use and decides nothing about permissions, which remain the authorization subject's (ADR-060 section 5). It takes no label and no fields, because the subject is a property of the Work Order being dispatched rather than a reference an author supplies. A type whose bindings reach this arm and which can only be filed by a schedule, trigger, mirror or the daemon is refused at validation, since such work has no delegation subject and can never acquire one. Exactly one of the spec or filer blocks must be declared (ADR-087 D4). |

**Exactly one of** `spec` | `filer`.

## `volumes` block

| Attribute | Type | Required | Default | Since | Constraints | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `volume` | block (list) | no | — | — | — | Data-volume mount declarations. A tool that declares NO writable volume still gets a working directory, and which directory that is depends on whether the host that ran the dispatch can reach the session's artifact volume: where it can — this daemon, and any placement that shares its disk — it is that volume, shared across the whole session, so a relative file written on one turn is readable on a later one; where it cannot — a fleet runner — it is that runner's own per-dispatch workspace, fresh for each dispatch and gone when it ends (ADR-038 Amendment 1 A1.3). The difference is deliberate: where a process runs is a workspace question. It is also invisible from inside the tool — the symptom is a missing file rather than an error — so the dispatch says which it got rather than leaving it to be discovered: the invocation record carries session_workspace = session_shared or per_dispatch (ADR-133 D18). Hand a file over explicitly instead, through the session file channel (sdk/toolsdk PublishSessionArtifact / ReadSessionArtifact), which answers with the bytes and behaves identically on both; or declare a writable volume here, which becomes the working directory on either machine. See docs/ops/tool-volume-bindings.md. |

## `volumes.volume` block

Nested under `volumes`. Repeatable.

| Attribute | Type | Required | Default | Since | Constraints | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `label` | string | yes | — | — | min length 1 | Volume binding label a work-order type's volumes { binding "<label>" {} } resolves. |
| `mount_path` | string | yes | — | — | — | Declared mount path. A label spelled like a path, not a path the tool can open: no sandbox backend relocates the directory, so the volume stays at its real host path. The runtime exports that host path as TOOL_VOLUME_<last segment>, and the executor symlinks the last segment into the working directory. Derive tool defaults from TOOL_VOLUME_*; never write this value down as a literal. |
| `writable` | boolean | no | — | — | — | Whether the mount is writable. Defaults to read-only. |
| `required` | boolean | no | — | — | — | Whether the tool refuses to run without this volume bound. |
| `tracked_checkout_input` | string | no | — | — | min length 1 | The name of the tool input whose value is the tracked checkout to mount, read-only, for each invocation (ADR-150 D11). This is the one way to bind a tracked checkout to a tool: it works the same for a call through the gateway and a call from a dispatch, and no work-order type declares a checkout binding. Refused at load beside writable = true, and refused unless it names a required string property of input_schema. See docs/subsystems/data-volumes.md. |
| `issue_extension` | boolean | no | — | — | — | Lets the dispatch issue a sandbox extension for this volume's own subtree, so a system service the tool hands the directory to may write there under the service's own sandbox (ADR-176 D5). The case it exists for is Metal's compiler service, which serializes Cycles' compiled kernels only where the client issued it an extension: a worker-scoped cache volume with this set keeps them across dispatches. ON DARWIN it emits (allow file-issue-extension (subpath <the volume's resolved path>)), bounded by that path and by nothing else; an issuance bounded by extension class alone is a measured sandbox escape and is never emitted. ON LINUX it is inert. Refused at load unless writable = true. Default false. |

## `checkpoints` block

| Attribute | Type | Required | Default | Since | Constraints | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `phases` | string[] | yes | — | — | — | The closed set of phases an invocation may report, in declaration order. Each is a KEY a consumer matches on rather than a label it prints, so whitespace and control characters are refused. A phase spelled other is refused by name: a catch-all inside a closed set is the free-text fallback the closed set exists to remove, since everything a producer would have narrated ends up under it. An empty list is legal and is the explicit statement that nothing here reports progress. Re-entering a phase is legal and expected — a retry genuinely re-enters the phase it failed in — and sequence numbers are monotonic, so the re-entry is visible as two records rather than one silently overwritten. |
| `payload_schema` | string | no | — | — | — | Raw JSON Schema for the domain payload — the half of a checkpoint the platform envelope has no field for (heredoc body in HCL). Omit it to declare none: a capability that declares no payload schema REFUSES a checkpoint carrying a payload, because the schema is the prescription and a payload nothing prescribes records a shape no consumer can read. No permissive stand-in is inferred. Refused outright when phases is empty, where it could never be consulted. IT MUST BE SELF-CONTAINED: an internal reference (#/$defs/...) is fine, and any $ref the compiler would have to fetch or read off the daemon's disk is refused, because the recipe is the declaration and a schema whose meaning lives in a second file is one no vault carries, no config plan diffs and no reviewer sees. Write it as a prescription rather than a permission: a checkpoint answers what would I want to know if this died right now, not what is happening, so artifact identity earns a place and a percentage-complete does not. |

## `acp` block

| Attribute | Type | Required | Default | Since | Constraints | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `attachments` | block | no | — | — | — | Optional interactive artifact reference transport. Omission preserves resource_link for existing bindings; no non-interactive framing changes. |
| `launch` | block | yes | — | — | — | How the inner harness process is started. Required: one acp-handler serves every ACP harness, so it has nothing to start until the recipe says what to start. |
| `capabilities` | string[] | yes | — | — | — | What this binding CLAIMS its harness advertises at initialize (ADR-115 D3). The handler checks the claim AGAINST the live response and never consults initialize in place of it: a capability the binding claims and the harness does not advertise REFUSES THE DISPATCH LOUDLY, before a turn is spent, because a binding that quietly ran with less than it declared would accept work it cannot honour and report nothing unusual. The opposite direction is not an error — a harness advertising more than the binding claims is an ordinary version moving forward, and nothing obliges a recipe to enumerate a surface it does not use. THE DECLARABLE VOCABULARY IS EXACTLY WHAT AN ACP initialize RESPONSE CAN ADVERTISE and is not restated in this schema: acp-handler derives it from the generated protocol types, so it moves when the protocol does, and a copy here would be a copy that stops matching — a recipe claiming a newly-added capability would be refused as a typo by a check pointing at the recipe for a defect in the schema. A misspelled name is still refused, by the handler, which prints the whole vocabulary when it does. A HARNESS'S CUSTOM SURFACE IS NOT IN THAT SET AND CANNOT BE: goose answers initialize with _meta: null and advertises none of its _goose/unstable/* methods, which is the observation that makes the declaration unavoidable rather than merely convenient — so a method a binding depends on is declared where it is USED, in the instructions and verb blocks, and what happens when one has moved is a method-not-found refusal at the call, naming the method. Required, and the EMPTY LIST IS THE LEGAL AND EXPECTED ANSWER for a harness that advertises nothing. |
| `capacity` | string | yes | — | — | one of `none` | What this binding can report about CONSUMPTION (ADR-115 D6). none is the whole vocabulary today and it is an HONEST DECLARED STATE RATHER THAN A DEFECT: goose reports no rate limit, no window and no reset anywhere on the ACP wire, and a BYOK harness pointed at an arbitrary endpoint has no account whose ceiling it could report. Required, with no default, for the reason every attribute of this block is required: an absent capacity and capacity = "none" would say the same thing to a scheduler and different things about the author, and D6's ruling is that a binding whose harness reports neither DECLARES it. DO NOT INVENT A METER FROM usage_update: what ACP carries is per-goal budget occupancy and spend, which is not an account meter, and a binding that reported one would be answering a scheduler's question with a different question's answer. ACP's per-goal budget meter is a later wave's arm; a value this set does not carry is refused here rather than accepted and ignored, because a class no handler reads is a declaration nothing honours. |
| `instructions` | block | yes | — | — | — | How ADR-108 D2's contract reaches a session, and WHEN IT IS RE-DELIVERED (ADR-115 D4). Required: a binding that delivers no contract cannot demonstrate that one arrived, and the demonstration is the point — the spike produced a selectable agent whose prompt SILENTLY NEVER APPLIED, where the selection succeeded, the harness listed the agent, nothing failed, and only the echo caught it. |
| `verb` | block (list) | no | — | — | — | How each in-flight verb this capability offers is performed against the harness (ADR-115 D5). Repeated; the block label is the verb. THIS BLOCK SAYS ONLY HOW. Whether a verb is offered at all is in_flight { accepts } 's single answer — read by the daemon — and this is read by the handler; the two MAY NOT DISAGREE and a recipe declaring a verb in one and not the other is refused at load, naming both sides. Declaring none is legal and means this capability offers no in-flight verb, which in_flight { accepts = [] } must then also say. |
